A1.justification: Both PDFs describe REGATE and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Retained material can be matched across restructuring and renumbering; no material reading gaps prevent comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original VideoLLaMA2 and VideoChat2 fine-tuning results, efficiency measurements, a weighting-factor ablation, and qualitative reference-loss examples.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds InternVL3.5 experiments, teacher-capacity ablations, memory and teacher-cost measurements, and attention visualizations.

M1.justification: The reference loss, student EMA, combined scoring, sparsity schedule, top-k gating, visual-token retention, and sparse decoder procedure remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 moves to the supplement. Applying REGATE to InternVL3.5 and explaining caching, gradients, and Q/K/V masking do not establish a changed algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same five image and eight video benchmarks and the same approximately 300,000-pair and 2.6-million-pair training subsets. InternVL3.5 uses the existing VideoChat2 training subset. Renamed benchmark labels and additional qualitative examples do not establish distinct task or domain coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds explicit comparisons using published LaVi scores on four video benchmarks and LLaVA-Meteor scores on three image benchmarks (Tables 5–6); v1 only discussed these methods in related work. InternVL3.5 with standard training also joins Tables 1–4 as a direct comparator. Existing comparator rows are retained.

E3.justification: v2 adds a 14B-model experiment using 16 H100 GPUs and a controlled teacher-capacity comparison using Qwen2-1.5B, 7B, and 57B teachers. Table 4 and the weighting-factor ablation change from MVBench accuracy to video-benchmark averages. Existing schedules, prompts, and 7B settings remain; converting their training times to GPU-hours does not indicate longer training.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether teacher capacity should match the student (Section 7.2, Table 8) and whether REGATE changes spatial attention (Figure 4). Figure 5 adds a third reference-loss example while retaining the original two. The existing weighting-factor ablation is retained with a revised accuracy aggregation.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or run-to-run error bars. The new benchmark averages and average memory measurements do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain the previous scores and add InternVL3.5 results, including MVBench accuracy of 68.3 without REGATE and 69.6 with it. v2 also adds teacher costs, memory measurements, comparator scores, learning curves, and teacher-capacity findings. The weighting ablation changes from 51.3/51.1/53.6 on MVBench to 47.7/46.4/48.9 averaged over video benchmarks; these are different reported metrics, not same-setting regressions.

T1.justification: Equations 1–4 and the top-k and mask definitions retain the same mathematical content. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs. The added teacher-capacity and tokenizer-alignment discussion provides qualitative reasoning and applicability guidance rather than a new formal derivation.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains parameter-free, architecture-preserving token gating for faster training with comparable or better accuracy. The abstract and introduction broaden the quantitative headline from VideoLLaMA2 using 35% of baseline tokens to three MLLMs using 38% on average, while retaining the up-to-2x speed claim.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of teacher-capacity mismatch, recommends capacity alignment, and states the need for compatible token boundaries. It also interprets attention localization and memory/communication savings. v1's dedicated large-scale limitations paragraph and future-work discussion are removed; the new 14B experiment only partly addresses the previously untested larger-model regimes.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies that teacher losses are computed once over the training dataset and cached, explains active-token Q/K/V gathering and backward masking, and documents the InternVL3.5 backbone and hardware. Teacher overhead and per-GPU memory are also disclosed. These materially expand implementation and resource information; code and models remain promised for future release.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to newer pruning, merging, and distillation work, including DivPrune, PACT, TAMP, and LLaVA-KD, while retaining the three related-work themes. Positioning against LaVi and Meteor gains empirical comparisons. Section 2.2 also corrects the description from gating both text and vision tokens to gating textual tokens while preserving visual tokens, consistent with the existing method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and model descriptions receive extensive rewriting. Detailed benchmark descriptions and the separate baseline subsection are condensed into Section 4.2. The conclusion is shortened, future-work and limitations sections disappear, and the appendices become reorganized numbered supplementary sections.

P2.justification: A new opening schematic replaces the lead learning-curve figure; the retained curve moves into a three-model Figure 3. v2 adds attention maps and comparison/teacher-capacity tables, expands the qualitative figure to three examples, and widens Table 4 with teacher-cost and memory columns. Algorithm 1 moves to the supplement, and the document is retypeset throughout.

improvement.justification: The added 14B validation, teacher-capacity study, masking details, and teacher-cost accounting strengthen evidence and transparency. However, v1's MVBench efficiency scores align with its benchmark table, whereas v2 introduces unexplained aggregate discrepancies: VideoLLaMA2-REGATE scores average about 52.0 across Tables 2–3, versus 48.9 reported in Tables 4 and 7. InternVL3.5-REGATE also has conflicting VizWiz scores in Tables 1 and 6 (61.5 versus 60.5). These reporting problems affect the new supporting evidence, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.
